title: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: If fuel/air ratio is proper and ignition timing is correct, the combustion process should be completed
choices: When the exhaust valve opens at the end of the power stroke.
Before top center on the compression stroke.
Just after top center at the beginning of the power stroke.
20 to 30° before top center at the end of the compression stroke.
questions.answerText: Just after top center at the beginning of the power stroke.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Ignition begins before top dead center so the flame has time to develop while the piston is near the end of compression. Peak pressure then occurs just after TDC, when it can push the piston down through the power stroke. Ignition timing is not the same instant as completed combustion.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: When is the fuel/air mixture ignited in a conventional reciprocating engine?
choices: When the piston reaches top dead center on the compression stroke.
After the piston passes top dead center on the power stroke.
When the piston has reached top dead center of the intake stroke.
Shortly before the piston reaches the top of the compression stroke.
questions.answerText: Shortly before the piston reaches the top of the compression stroke.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
The spark is timed shortly before TDC on the compression stroke. The burning mixture takes finite time to reach peak pressure, so starting combustion before TDC places peak pressure just after TDC for useful expansion work.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: The primary purpose in setting proper valve timing and overlap is to
choices: obtain the best volumetric efficiency and lower cylinder operating temperatures.
Eliminate the need to coordinate ignition timing with valve movement.
Permit the best possible charge of fuel/air mixture into the cylinders.
Gain more thorough exhaust gas scavenging.
questions.answerText: obtain the best volumetric efficiency and lower cylinder operating temperatures.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Correct valve timing lets the intake charge continue filling the cylinder and helps clear hot exhaust gas during overlap. Better volumetric efficiency improves charge mass, while effective scavenging reduces retained hot gas and cylinder temperature. Excessive overlap or mistiming can instead cause reversion.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Into what part of a reciprocating engine induction system is deicing alcohol normally injected?
choices: Into the fuel bowl downstream of the throttle plate.
The airstream ahead of the carburetor.
The low-pressure area ahead of the throttle valve.
questions.answerText: The airstream ahead of the carburetor.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Alcohol is injected into the airstream ahead of the carburetor so it can reach the inlet and carburetor passages where ice may form. The alcohol lowers water's freezing point; it is not sprayed into the cylinders as a combustion additive.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: During full power output of an unsupercharged engine equipped with a float-type carburetor, in which of the following areas will the highest pressure exist?
choices: Downstream of the throttle valve in the intake manifold.
questions.answerText: Carburetor air scoop.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
In a normally aspirated induction system at full power, the carburetor air scoop is exposed to ram pressure and is upstream of the pressure drop across the carburetor venturi and throttle. Thus it has the highest pressure among the listed locations.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Augmenter tubes are part of which reciprocating engine system?
questions.answerText: Exhaust.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Augmenter tubes use the high-velocity exhaust flow to induce additional cooling air through the engine compartment. They are part of the exhaust arrangement and use an ejector effect; they are not fuel-metering tubes.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Which of the following assists in removing heat from the metal walls and fins of an air-cooled cylinder assembly?
questions.answerText: A baffle and cowl arrangement.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Baffles and the cowling direct cooling air across cylinder fins instead of letting it bypass the hot surfaces. The metal fins increase heat-transfer area, and forced airflow carries heat away. A missing or poorly sealed baffle can cause localized overheating.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: If the intake valve is opened too early in the cycle of operation of a four-stroke cycle engine, it may result in
questions.answerText: backfiring into the induction system.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
If the intake valve opens too early while cylinder pressure is still high, combustion gases can escape backward into the induction passage. Correct valve timing keeps the intake event coordinated with piston motion and exhaust pressure.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What is the purpose of a power check on a reciprocating engine?
choices: To determine if the fuel/air mixture is adequate.
To determine whether the engine develops its specified power under the test conditions.
questions.answerText: To determine satisfactory performance.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
A power check compares the engine's measured indications and output with specified performance limits. It can reveal inadequate power or abnormal operation, but it is a performance assessment rather than a single-component diagnosis.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Backfiring through the carburetor generally results from the use of _____.
choices: equal amount of fuel and air
questions.answerText: an excessively lean mixture
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
A lean mixture can burn slowly and irregularly; flame may continue into the intake event and ignite mixture in the induction passage, causing backfire. A rich mixture more commonly causes roughness, fouling, or reduced power.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: The following are the major components of a normally aspirated engine except _____.
questions.answerText: ice removal system
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
The listed major engine systems include induction, fuel metering, ignition, lubrication, cooling, and exhaust. An ice-removal system is an accessory or installation feature, not a fundamental engine component system present on every reciprocating engine.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: A fuel ratio of 11:1 normally refers to _____.
choices: 1 part of fuel, 11 parts of air
1.1 part of fuel, 1 part of air
questions.answerText: 1 part of fuel, 11 parts of air
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
A ratio written fuel-to-air as 11:1 means one unit of fuel for eleven units of air. Always read which material is named first; reversing the order changes the mixture interpretation.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Reciprocating engine power will be decreased at all altitudes if _____.
questions.answerText: humidity is increased
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Higher humidity means more water vapor occupies part of the inducted gas mixture, displacing some oxygen for a given volume. With less oxygen available for combustion, power decreases, particularly in a normally aspirated engine.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: The device that controls the volume of the fuel/air mixture to the cylinders is called a _____.
questions.answerText: throttle valve
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
The throttle valve regulates the amount of mixture or air admitted to the engine and therefore controls power. The mixture control changes fuel-to-air proportion; it is not the primary airflow-volume control.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: How does a float-type carburetor normally meter fuel into the airstream?
choices: Fuel drains by gravity into the exhaust
A pressure difference draws fuel from a metering discharge nozzle
A high-pressure injector sprays fuel at each spark plug
questions.answerText: A pressure difference draws fuel from a metering discharge nozzle
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Fuel flows from the float chamber through a metering path because pressure at the discharge nozzle is lower than the fuel supply pressure. The pressure difference draws and atomizes fuel into the moving airstream; the float maintains a nearly constant fuel level.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What is the purpose of the carburetor venturi?
choices: Increase local air velocity and lower static pressure to promote fuel discharge
Heat the fuel above its boiling point
questions.answerText: Increase local air velocity and lower static pressure to promote fuel discharge
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
The venturi narrows the passage, increasing airflow velocity and lowering local static pressure. That pressure drop helps draw fuel through the discharge nozzle. It does not raise pressure to force fuel into the airstream.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Why is mixture leaned as altitude increases in a carbureted engine?
choices: Air density decreases, so less fuel is needed to maintain the proper mixture
questions.answerText: Air density decreases, so less fuel is needed to maintain the proper mixture
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
As altitude increases, air density and oxygen mass per intake volume decrease. The same fuel flow would make the mixture too rich, so the pilot reduces fuel with the mixture control to preserve the proper fuel-air ratio.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What is the function of an accelerator pump in a carburetor?
choices: Temporarily enrich the mixture when the throttle is opened rapidly
questions.answerText: Temporarily enrich the mixture when the throttle is opened rapidly
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Rapid throttle opening increases airflow immediately, while fuel delivery may lag. The accelerator pump supplies a brief extra shot of fuel to prevent a transient lean stumble; it is not the normal steady-state metering circuit.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What does a carburetor economizer or power-enrichment system do at high power?
choices: Adds fuel to provide the richer mixture required for high-power operation
questions.answerText: Adds fuel to provide the richer mixture required for high-power operation
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
At high power the engine needs a richer mixture for detonation margin and cooling. The economizer or power-enrichment circuit adds fuel when the throttle reaches the high-power region; it does not lean the mixture for cruise.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What is the purpose of an idle system in a carburetor?
choices: Meter fuel when airflow through the main venturi is too low for normal main-nozzle operation
questions.answerText: Meter fuel when airflow through the main venturi is too low for normal main-nozzle operation
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
At idle, airflow through the main venturi is too small to create enough pressure drop for the main discharge nozzle. The idle circuit supplies metered fuel through ports near the throttle plate, where local pressure conditions support flow.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What is a common effect of carburetor icing?
choices: A gradual loss of power and possible roughness as ice restricts airflow
questions.answerText: A gradual loss of power and possible roughness as ice restricts airflow
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Ice can form in the carburetor throat as pressure and temperature fall during fuel vaporization. Accumulating ice restricts airflow and may cause gradual RPM or manifold-pressure loss and roughness. Carburetor heat warms the inlet air to melt or prevent this ice.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Why does carburetor heat usually reduce engine power when applied?
choices: Heated air is less dense and may also bypass the normal intake path
questions.answerText: Heated air is less dense and may also bypass the normal intake path
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Heated induction air has lower density, so each cylinder receives less oxygen mass at a given volume. Carburetor heat can also add intake restriction. The immediate power reduction is expected and is distinct from the power recovery after ice melts.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: In a pressure-injection carburetor, what provides the pressure for fuel delivery?
choices: A fuel pump and metering unit
Only gravity in a float bowl
questions.answerText: A fuel pump and metering unit
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
A pressure-injection carburetor uses a pump and metering unit to pressurize and regulate fuel delivery. Fuel flow is controlled by pressure differentials and metering components rather than being drawn solely from a float-bowl level.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: An air-to-fuel mass ratio of 12:1 means what?
choices: Twelve units of pressure per fuel unit
Twelve parts air by mass for one part fuel by mass
Twelve parts fuel by mass for one part air
questions.answerText: Twelve parts air by mass for one part fuel by mass
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
An air-to-fuel mass ratio of 12:1 specifies twelve units of air mass for each one unit of fuel mass. It is a mass ratio, not a volume ratio, and the order is air first, fuel second.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an intake manifold?
choices: Distribute the combustible charge to the engine cylinders
questions.answerText: Distribute the combustible charge to the engine cylinders
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
The intake manifold carries and distributes the combustible charge from the carburetor or fuel-metering system to individual cylinders. Unequal distribution can produce different cylinder mixtures and temperatures.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What can an induction leak downstream of a carburetor cause?
choices: A lower compression ratio by design
An excessively lean mixture and uneven cylinder operation
An enriched mixture in all cases
questions.answerText: An excessively lean mixture and uneven cylinder operation
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
A leak downstream of the carburetor admits unmetered air. Since the fuel system does not add fuel for that extra air, the affected cylinders run lean and may operate unevenly, especially at idle.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: How does a fuel-injection system differ from a float carburetor at the cylinder?
choices: It meters oil instead of fuel
Fuel is metered under pressure and distributed through injector nozzles
Fuel is mixed only in a float bowl
questions.answerText: Fuel is metered under pressure and distributed through injector nozzles
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Fuel injection meters fuel under pressure and routes it through injector nozzles near the intake ports or cylinders. A float carburetor meters fuel into the common airflow using venturi pressure changes and a float-controlled supply.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Why are alternate-air doors provided on some induction systems?
choices: Provide an alternate source of induction air if the normal inlet is obstructed
questions.answerText: Provide an alternate source of induction air if the normal inlet is obstructed
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
An alternate-air door lets the engine draw air from another source if the normal inlet or filter is blocked. The alternate path preserves airflow but may be unfiltered or warmer, depending on the installation.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: What is the effect of a restricted air filter on a normally aspirated engine?
choices: Reduced induction airflow and available power
Higher volumetric efficiency in all conditions
questions.answerText: Reduced induction airflow and available power
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
A restricted filter limits the mass of air entering a normally aspirated engine. Less oxygen is available to burn fuel, reducing maximum power; a sufficiently severe restriction may also cause rough operation.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Why is fuel vaporization important before combustion?
choices: It helps produce a combustible mixture that can burn consistently
It prevents the fuel from mixing with air
It raises the engine’s mechanical compression ratio
It removes the need for ignition
questions.answerText: It helps produce a combustible mixture that can burn consistently
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Fuel must be atomized and vaporized sufficiently to mix with air and burn steadily. Poor vaporization can cause uneven distribution, incomplete combustion, and difficulty operating, especially during cold conditions.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: During a bench test, an engine receives 900 lb of air per hour and 75 lb of fuel per hour. What is the air-to-fuel mass ratio?
questions.explanation:
**Worked solution**
Air-to-fuel mass ratio = air mass flow / fuel mass flow = 900 lb/hr / 75 lb/hr = 12. The hourly units cancel, so the ratio is 12:1 by mass.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: An engine requires an air-to-fuel mass ratio of 15:1. If air flow is 1,200 lb/hr, what fuel flow is required?
questions.explanation:
**Worked solution**
For an air-to-fuel ratio of 15:1, fuel flow = air flow / 15 = 1,200 lb/hr / 15 = 80 lb/hr. Check: 15 x 80 = 1,200 lb/hr of air.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: A test cell measures 180 kg/hr of air and 15 kg/hr of fuel. Find the air-to-fuel ratio.
questions.explanation:
**Worked solution**
Air-to-fuel mass ratio = 180 kg/hr / 15 kg/hr = 12. The flow units cancel; this means 12 kg of air per kilogram of fuel.
tags: Reciprocating Induction, Carburetion, and Fuel Metering

questions.question: Which of the following will decrease volumetric efficiency in a reciprocating engine? 1. Full throttle operation. 2. Low cylinder head temperatures. 3. Improper valve timing. 4. Sharp bends in the induction system. 5. High carburetor air temperatures.
questions.explanation:
**Why this is correct**
Improper valve timing and sharp induction bends reduce the volume of fresh charge reaching the cylinders. High carburetor-air temperature lowers air density, also reducing inducted mass. Wide-open throttle and a cooler cylinder head generally support, rather than reduce, volumetric efficiency in the conditions assumed by this question.
